  - heading "You said My child knows letter sounds but cannot read words. Why?" [level=5]
  - paragraph: My child knows letter sounds but cannot read words. Why?
  - button "Copy prompt":
    - img: copy
  - button "Edit":
    - img: edit
  - heading "Gemini said" [level=6]
  - paragraph: This is one of the most common and puzzling stages in early literacy development. It can feel frustrating when a child seems to have all the "pieces"—they know what s says and what a says—but they can't put them together to say "sat."
  - paragraph: Knowing letter sounds is a crucial foundation, but reading actual words requires a completely different neurological skill called blending and phonological processing.
  - heading "Why Your Child May Be Stuck" [level=3]
  - list:
    - paragraph: The Gap Between Isolation and Synthesis Knowing a sound in isolation (seeing m and saying /mmm/) is different from holding three sounds in your head simultaneously and blending them together smoothly into a spoken word (moving from /m/ - /a/ - /t/ to "mat").
    - paragraph: Phonological Blending Deficit Some children struggle with auditory blending before they even try print. If you say the separate sounds out loud—like "f-i-sh"—can your child tell you the word is "fish"? If they struggle to blend sounds when heard orally, they will naturally struggle to blend them when seeing letters on a page.
    - paragraph: Working Memory Overload Reading a simple three-letter word requires a child's brain to look at a letter, recall its sound, hold that sound in mind while looking at the next letter, recall its sound, and so on, until the end of the word. If this process takes too much effort, the beginning of the word is forgotten by the time they reach the end.
    - paragraph: Rote Memorization vs. True Phonics Sometimes children memorize letter sounds visually or through songs without fully connecting the abstract symbol to its phonetic function. They may identify the letter name or sound quickly out of habit, but the cognitive bridge to decoding hasn't been built yet.
  - heading "Actionable Ways to Help" [level=3]
  - list:
    - paragraph: "Practice Oral Blending (Sound Games) Before asking your child to read words on paper, play blending games without letters. Say sounds slowly and ask them to guess the word. (Example: \"Can you touch your h-a-t?\" or \"What is this animal? d-o-g\".) This trains the ear and brain to synthesize sounds without the added stress of looking at letters."
    - paragraph: "Use Continuous Blending (Stretching Sounds) Traditional phonics often teaches choppy sounds: /s/ ... /a/ ... /t/. For a struggling beginner, this makes blending harder. Instead, teach continuous blending by stretching the sounds so they flow into each other without stopping, especially with continuant sounds like m, s, f, l, n:"
    - list:
      - paragraph: "Instead of: /s/ (pause) /a/ (pause) /t/"
      - paragraph: "Try: Sssss-aaaa-t (sliding your finger smoothly underneath the letters without lifting it)."
    - paragraph: Start with Two-Letter Words Three-letter words (CVC words like cat or pig) can be overwhelming at first. Step back to two-letter "word families" or continuous blending pairs first, such as at, in, up, am, or on. Once they can blend two sounds effortlessly, add the third.
    - paragraph: Use Tactile and Visual Prompts
    - list:
      - paragraph: "Elkonin Boxes (Sound Boxes): Draw three boxes on a paper. Put a token in each box for each sound in \"dog\" (/d/ - /o/ - /g/), pushing a token into each box as you make the sound."
      - paragraph: "Finger Sliding: Have them point to the first letter, hold the sound, and slide their finger continuously across a line underneath the word to the final letter."
  - paragraph: Would you like some specific, multi-step activities or recommended simple books you can use at home to help bridge this gap?
